bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Dependence on government contracts and scheme funding — Most revenue comes from contracts awarded by central and state governments and local authorities under schemes such as AMRUT, Jal Jeevan Mission, Namami Gange and PMGSY. The order book therefore depends on government budgets and policy priorities. Spending cuts, tender delays, changed pre-qualification rules or cancelled projects could shrink the pipeline.
- Working-capital intensity and long receivable cycles — Upfront procurement and mobilisation costs, milestone-based billing subject to government certification, performance guarantees backed by cash margins, and retention money held until defect-liability periods end all tie up liquidity. The company may have to rely on short-term borrowings at higher interest cost.
- Project execution risk — Strict timelines, technical specifications, approvals, land acquisition, labour availability and site constraints can cause cost overruns, penalties, invoked performance securities or delayed certification of work.
- Monsoon and extreme-weather disruption — Heavy rainfall, floods, cyclones and other extreme weather can halt construction and pipe-laying, damage sites and equipment, and push revenue and profit into later quarters.
- Policy and regulatory uncertainty — Changes in government regulations, contract frameworks or environmental norms could delay or alter project scopes, affecting revenue projections and execution timelines.
- Intensifying competition — Large conglomerates and niche technology players are both competing harder in infrastructure, which could bring pricing pressure and lower margins.
- Manpower, supply-chain and safety challenges — Shortages of skilled personnel, delays in material supply chains and safety incidents in high-risk construction zones can slow projects or cause cost overruns.
- Technological obsolescence — As infrastructure becomes more digitised, fast technology change risks obsolescence unless the company keeps investing in innovation and upskilling.

business.body: Technocraft Ventures executes turnkey engineering, procurement and construction (EPC) contracts across wastewater treatment, water supply schemes, operation and maintenance of public utilities, electrical transmission and distribution networks and substations, roads and highways, microtunnelling and sector-level urban development. Its clients are mainly state governments, public works departments, urban local bodies and other government agencies, and contracts are won predominantly by tender under central and state schemes. It also takes on stand-alone O&M contracts for treatment plants, sewer networks and road projects, and residential building work as part of its urban infrastructure business.
business.title: What they do

business.body:
- **Water & wastewater:** Wastewater treatment (WWT) EPC, Water supply scheme projects (WSSPs), Sewerage networks
- **Operation & Maintenance (O&M):** O&M of public utilities: plant operation, preventive and corrective maintenance, equipment monitoring, process optimisation, sludge management, routine inspections
- **Electrical:** Electrical transmission and distribution networks, Construction of substations
- **Roads & highways:** Road and highway works
- **Urban infrastructure:** Residential building construction, Sector-level urban development
- **Microtunnelling:** Microtunnelling

outlook.body:
- Keep internal accruals to fund business needs and growth instead of paying dividends; no dividend was recommended for the year under review.
- Listed on the BSE and NSE main boards (trading from August 14, 2026) through an IPO that combined a fresh issue with an offer for sale by the selling shareholder M/s. Kartikey Constructions.
outlook.title: Strategy & capital allocation

outlook.body: No manufacturing capacity or capex programme is disclosed; this is an asset-light EPC contractor. Growth is described as footprint expansion: the company sees an opportunity to expand across more Indian states and into new verticals such as industrial water management and the private sector, and to pursue PPP models. Current execution examples include an ongoing Delhi Jal Board project laying water transmission mains from the Bhagirathi Water Treatment Plant with microtunnelling technology, and a recently awarded contract to widen and strengthen a state road in Saharanpur district (Uttar Pradesh) up to the Uttarakhand border.

financial_valuation.risk: Our business is significantly dependent on contracts awarded by Government authorities under Government programmes, and any failure or delay in securing, executing or collecting payments under such contracts could materially and adversely affect our business, financial condition, cash flows and results of operations.
Delays in certification of work done, disputes on variation claims, or fiscal constraints of the awarding authority can lead to extended collection timelines and working capital pressures.
Any adverse outcome in these proceedings may have an adverse impact on our profitability and cash flows.

internal_operational.risk: Unforeseen factors such as adverse weather, land acquisition delays, labour availability and supply chain disruptions may also materially affect execution schedules.
Certain delays, which were not attributable to our Company, resulted in deductions and the levy of liquidated damages by the client, which were disputed by us.

Our Company has not experienced any receivable write-offs or disputes on bills with customers to date except we have initiated arbitration proceedings vide Case No. 02 of 2021 pursuing the recovery of additional claims aggregating approximately ₹ 50.15 million and are also contesting the revised liquidated damages of ₹ 5.39 million imposed by RUIDP.

strategy_growth.risk: O&M work is resource-intensive and spread across geographically dispersed locations.
The availability, skill level and cost of such sub-contractors’ deployed workmen vary across geographies and may be influenced by seasonal factors or competing infrastructure demands.

In parallel, water treatment and reuse technologies are evolving rapidly, with new processes and equipment being introduced by original equipment manufacturers (“OEMs”) and international technology providers.

one_liner.title: One Liner (RHP)
one_liner.body: Multidisciplinary public-infrastructure EPC contractor that wins tender-based water, wastewater, power-distribution, road and urban-development contracts from state governments and agencies across Northern India.

business_model.title: What they do
business_model.body: Technocraft Ventures executes turnkey engineering, procurement and construction (EPC) contracts across wastewater treatment, water supply schemes, operation and maintenance of public utilities, electrical transmission and distribution networks and substations, roads and highways, microtunnelling and sector-level urban development. Its clients are mainly state governments, public works departments, urban local bodies and other government agencies, and contracts are won predominantly by tender under central and state schemes. It also takes on stand-alone O&M contracts for treatment plants, sewer networks and road projects, and residential building work as part of its urban infrastructure business.

group_structure.title: Group structure (subsidiaries / JV / related parties)
group_structure.body:
- TESPL LRS TCPL - JV — associate: Joint-venture associate; the company books revenue from operations from it and records its share of profit/loss.
- Krishna TCPL - JV — associate: Former joint-venture associate, dissolved on 31 December 2024 by a dissolution deed.
- VVIP Infratech Limited (formerly Vibhor Vaibhav Infra Private Limited) — related party: Counterparty for purchase and job-work transactions.
- Sanjay Tyagi HUF — related party: HUF whose Karta is the Managing Director; has lent to the company.
- Neeraj Tyagi HUF — related party: HUF whose Karta is the Managing Director's brother.

products.title: Products & brands
products.body:
- **Water & wastewater:** Wastewater treatment (WWT) EPC, Water supply scheme projects (WSSPs), Sewerage networks
- **Operation & Maintenance (O&M):** O&M of public utilities: plant operation, preventive and corrective maintenance, equipment monitoring, process optimisation, sludge management, routine inspections
- **Electrical:** Electrical transmission and distribution networks, Construction of substations
- **Roads & highways:** Road and highway works
- **Urban infrastructure:** Residential building construction, Sector-level urban development
- **Microtunnelling:** Microtunnelling

end_markets.title: End Markets (RHP)
end_markets.body:
- State governments and government agencies, public works departments and urban local bodies (tender-based)
- Northern India: Uttar Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Rajasthan and the National Capital Territory of Delhi
- Central and state schemes: AMRUT, JNNURM, UIDSSMT, Namami Gange, Jal Jeevan Mission, Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana
- Projects funded by multilateral agencies (Asian Development Bank, World Bank)

capital_allocation.title: Strategy & capital allocation
capital_allocation.body:
- Keep internal accruals to fund business needs and growth instead of paying dividends; no dividend was recommended for the year under review.
- Listed on the BSE and NSE main boards (trading from August 14, 2026) through an IPO that combined a fresh issue with an offer for sale by the selling shareholder M/s. Kartikey Constructions.

capex_expansion.title: Capex & expansion plans
capex_expansion.body: No manufacturing capacity or capex programme is disclosed; this is an asset-light EPC contractor. Growth is described as footprint expansion: the company sees an opportunity to expand across more Indian states and into new verticals such as industrial water management and the private sector, and to pursue PPP models. Current execution examples include an ongoing Delhi Jal Board project laying water transmission mains from the Bhagirathi Water Treatment Plant with microtunnelling technology, and a recently awarded contract to widen and strengthen a state road in Saharanpur district (Uttar Pradesh) up to the Uttarakhand border.

moat.title: Bull — competitive strengths
moat.body: - Regulatory-Approved Electrical works Capabilities with Statewide Licenses

risks.title: Bear — key risks
risks.body:
- Dependence on government contracts and scheme funding — Most revenue comes from contracts awarded by central and state governments and local authorities under schemes such as AMRUT, Jal Jeevan Mission, Namami Gange and PMGSY. The order book therefore depends on government budgets and policy priorities. Spending cuts, tender delays, changed pre-qualification rules or cancelled projects could shrink the pipeline.
- Working-capital intensity and long receivable cycles — Upfront procurement and mobilisation costs, milestone-based billing subject to government certification, performance guarantees backed by cash margins, and retention money held until defect-liability periods end all tie up liquidity. The company may have to rely on short-term borrowings at higher interest cost.
- Project execution risk — Strict timelines, technical specifications, approvals, land acquisition, labour availability and site constraints can cause cost overruns, penalties, invoked performance securities or delayed certification of work.
- Monsoon and extreme-weather disruption — Heavy rainfall, floods, cyclones and other extreme weather can halt construction and pipe-laying, damage sites and equipment, and push revenue and profit into later quarters.
- Policy and regulatory uncertainty — Changes in government regulations, contract frameworks or environmental norms could delay or alter project scopes, affecting revenue projections and execution timelines.
- Intensifying competition — Large conglomerates and niche technology players are both competing harder in infrastructure, which could bring pricing pressure and lower margins.
- Manpower, supply-chain and safety challenges — Shortages of skilled personnel, delays in material supply chains and safety incidents in high-risk construction zones can slow projects or cause cost overruns.
- Technological obsolescence — As infrastructure becomes more digitised, fast technology change risks obsolescence unless the company keeps investing in innovation and upskilling.
